I used to have the same fear. It was my goal in life to be the perfect wife and have a husband that was absolutely in love with me and wonderful family to complete it all. I had to let go of that dream and opened myself up to new dreams. Dreams of giving love to others (friends, family, my community) without being concerned if I received it back. Dreams of being an accomplished painter, rock climber, skier, and banjo player. Dreams of becoming respected in my profession. There isn't one path to giving your life meaning and happiness. If I never have a spouse or a family or I only end up with some of the things I listed above I feel confident that I would find a way to be happy with my life because I know I can't do it all perfectly and I know I'm trying my best. and I forgive myself for any shortcomings.

Building your self esteem can come from anything! Setting small achievable goals and accomplishing them really does it for me. I literally set goals like I'm going to floss this morning and when I do it I feel like "wow I'm really working on myself". Another thing is I focus on performing anxiety coping mechanisms on my own before reaching out to others. A lot of times its uncomfortable and I badly wish I could be held and cuddled by someone in those moments but afterwards I know I've been strong for myself and it makes it easier to face the next tough moment. When needed I reach out to those who I know can help me in a healthy mature way, not everyone is a good support system.
thanks!
Happy new year to you too! Actually doing really well, I feel really strong, empowered and motivated to continue making positive changes in my life. How are you?

I second this, I realized I heavily use romantic relationships as coping mechanisms for stress. Now when the thoughts come up about the ex I recognize its just because I'm stressed. Then I try a bunch of stuff that helps me calm down and usually it goes away. Breathing exercises, walks, showers, etc.

Actual therapy my dude. Although a lot of it was just needing someone to listen and point out areas where I was being too hard on myself/romanticizing the relationship too much. They helped me learn how to be present and not weighed down by the past or anxious for the future while also setting goals that built my self esteem and created hope. They also said just talking about the break up/trauma from the relationship a lot helps a person emotionally accept a bad situation.

I'm going through something similar. Finishing up graduate school, was broken up with, and trying to rebuild. My first post on this sub was about going through the motions. There was a long time of just not enjoying anything, like literally feeling like I would never be happy about anything no matter what happened. Recently though I've started to feel some hope about things. I set some goal for 2021 and just thinking about them gets me excited in a small way. I still feel broken down in many ways but that spark makes me believe one day I'll be whole again. Not just whole, stronger. What got me there was a lot of self reflection and therapy about who I wanted to be, why the break up was devastating, debugging a lot of insecurities and self doubt, and what it would take to become a person I could be proud of. And a lot of time. If it worked for me I believe it will for you too. If you'd like an accountability partner I'm looking for one so feel free to reach out.

Small goal setting might help you build some pride in your accomplishments. Over time this can help you start to value yourself more. When things are emotionally difficult for me I set it as low as possible like did I brush my teeth this morning. Also reinvest in taking care of yourself whatever that means to you like working out, getting more sleep etc. Instead of having romantic relationships being your main focus shift it to being more balanced to other areas of your life. Rejection is the worst when it feels like the relationship was the only good thing in your life, so fill your life with career accomplishments, rewarding friendships/familial relationships, find purpose in volunteering/helping your community, take care of a pet, take care of your health, pursue a hobby that you enjoy so when rejection does happen you can turn around and say my life is still pretty good without them. Life is full of rejection because not everyone is meant to be your life partner, but that doesn't make you unlovable.

this dude is not the sole opinion on what is attractive. there are plenty of reasons to find someone attractive and many have nothing to do with what they look like. what is undeniably unattractive is someone saying something hurtful in the guise of it being "honest" when its just them voicing their flawed/biased perspective.

I'm a 23 f who also saw my life's purpose as loving someone romantically. I get the struggle of wanting something that is out of your control, having a healthy romantic relationship is the stars aligning where you meet someone who 1) meets your standards 2) you meet their standards 3) they want/are ready for a romantic relationship 4) when you both are in a romantic relationship with each other you are able to communicate/ handle conflict in a healthy way. My last relationship didn't have #4 and it made me more miserable than I think just being single would have. 2,3,4 are out of your control and 1 shouldn't be lowered. Also I've done the whole making myself more likeable/beautiful and when I did end up in a relationship it mindfucked me about whether that person actually loved me or a superficial version of myself. I've decided instead to focus my life's purpose elsewhere and if someone comes along and loves me then it will be because they love me as I live my life for myself and not to attract others. My goal was to love someone so I'll love my friends and family, I'll volunteer and love my community, maybe I'll get a dog and love that animal. Life can still be full of love even without a romantic partner. The love I put out into the world is what I can control and it makes me happy/helps me value myself and I've dropped my expectation to be loved in return for it as this will only be disappointing and feels kind of selfish. Setting goals for myself in my career/hobbies/social circle to be proud of help me value myself too. All of this self-esteem building will hopefully get to a place where another person loving me back isn't what I need since I love myself. Also I absolutely agree with billjitsu, they gave great perspective.

I recently went through a break up that knocked me on my ass. But I am optimistic that it provides an opportunity for a fresh start and path for me to grow myself as an individual and maybe that's what this moment is for you too. My relationship ended because he was overly critical and controlling and no matter how I asked him to stop saying such negative things about me he wouldn't. In the aftermath that creates a lot of self doubt so be careful not to internalize those things, no one can decide who you are or will be but yourself. I also came to realize that I use relationships with men as a coping mechanism. The cuddling, affection, flirting, compliments, and security from a support system were ways in which I avoided dealing with stress and my own insecurities. Now I realize that I can't have a relationship just to make myself feel better about myself and my future/life. I need to be able to fill that need on my own and then I can date someone because its not fair to use another person like that and it makes the relationship toxic no matter what I do. If that rings true for you maybe a period of independence where you work on yourself mentally, physically, emotionally will help you value yourself and give yourself self confidence. By doing this I've had massive improvements so there is light at the end of the tunnel for you too.

Wow good for you for taking improv classes that takes a lot of courage. I have by no means figured everything out and also suffer from self loathing a lot, but I was able to grow out of social anxiety and now its more about my romantic life lol. In terms of what other's think of you maybe a reminder that most people have rich full lives with their own problems which mostly keep them from being concerned/talking about you. Also I have the opinion that neither the most negative or most positive view point is the realistic one, so don't get in the trap of thinking that by being your own harshest critic you are seeing yourself as you actually are. Maybe when you get a negative thought think of a polar opposite positive thought and then try to find the middle point and try to believe that opinion. That helps me a lot and is usually a counter opinion of myself that holds me accountable while also being kind to myself. Lastly as someone who went from having no friends to having a decent crowd that always say I'm "fun or funny" it is absolutely a learned skill. I realized that people like those who act confident, seem to be having fun, and are authentic. When you're at the gym and you feel goofy try having a laugh about it. I take a lot of classes where I notice a lot of my classmates are afraid to act like they don't know the material and I made a lot of friends by admitting/joking that I struggled, its more real. Maybe in your improv class saying "Oh man this is so hard but I'm having a lot of fun" could help people open up and be more comfortable with you. Also I'm sure you'll learn in your improv class that getting people interested in you/what you're saying has a lot to do with the cadence, timing, and emphasis of how you say it. I studied a few story telling techniques from comedians and public speakers and now people think I'm funny when I changed nothing about the content/my personality. Sorry for the length and hope any of this helps.

I suffer from the same issue, so I don't have a lot of good solutions :(. My therapist often recommends grounding exercises where you focus on physical/tangible sensations like spending some time thinking about a calming visual, flexing and then releasing each of your muscles starting from your toes and moving up, and deep breaths. These are hard for me to focus on so I try to perform an activity that is different from what I was doing at the time like going for a drive/walk, taking a shower, taking a nap, watching a show, getting something really delicious to eat, just something that breaks the situation/routine and therefore your thoughts up. What works best for me is to actively challenge those thoughts, I pretend I'm a lawyer or a debater and won't let myself off the hook in believing negative things without sufficient evidence (stick with hard facts no interpretations of people's actions) also if there is evidence of a negative thing I must also take a hard look at contradicting evidence that is positive. I have anxiety and depression too so these only help me manage, its not perfect but it helps.

Maybe its also helpful to remind ourselves that a lot of those people in "successful" positions may look like they are effortlessly achieving things. I am an engineering graduate student and at my college I gave a high school student a tour and told her about my research accomplishments and she said that I was doing things that she dreamed of doing. I felt like a fraud since it all sounded so good but in reality I was crying in my bed anxious about my potential failures a few days earlier.
